metadata.title: Ramdass v. Angelone, 530 U.S. 156 (2000) (No. 99-7000)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Ramdass v. Angelone

Opinion filed: 2000-06-12

Docket No.: 99-7000

Citations:
• 147 L. Ed. 2d 125
• 120 S. Ct. 2113
• 530 U.S. 156
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 3965

Case holding summaries:
• describing Simmons' premise and plurality opinion
• parole eligibility instruction required “only ... [in] instances where, as a legal matter, there is no possibility of parole if the jury decides the 18 appropriate sentence is life in prison”
• "Simmons applies only to instances where, as a legal matter, there is no possibility of parole if the jury decides the appropriate sentence is life in prison."
• stating that "[s]tates have some discretion in determining the extent to which a sentencing jury should be advised of probable future custody and parole status in a future dangerousness case"
• plurality opinion of Kennedy, J.
• considering a Virginia sen- tencing scheme and holding that a Simmons instruction was not required
• "Simmons does not require courts to estimate the likelihood of future contingencies concerning the defendant's parole ineligibility."
• refusing to accept Ramdass's argument that the Court should "ignore the legal rules dictating his parole eligibility under state law in favor of . . . a functional approach, under which. . . a court evalu- ates whether it looks like the defendant will turn out to be parole ineligible"
• " Simmons applies only to instances where, as a legal matter, there is no possibility of parole if the jury decides the appropriate sentence is life in prison."
• plurality opinion of Kennedy, J., in which Rehnquist, C.J., and Scalia and Thomas, JJ. join
• “The parole-ineligibility instruction is required only when [in a capital case], assuming the jury fixes the sentence at life, the defendant is ineligible for parole under state law.”
• explaining that when material differences exist between cases, the state court's decision in the case pending review is not contrary to the rule announced in the previous case from the United States Supreme Court
• "If the inquiry is to include whether a defendant will, at some point, be released from prison, even the age or health of a prisoner facing a long period of incarceration would seem relevant. The possibilities are many, the certainties few."
